rag.content:
/-- The disjoint union of finsets is a sum -/
def Finset.union (s t : Finset α) (h : Disjoint s t) :
    s ⊕ t ≃ (s ∪ t : Finset α) :=
  Equiv.Set.ofEq (coe_union _ _) |>.trans (Equiv.Set.union (disjoint_coe.mpr h)) |>.symm

rag.name: Complementeds.disjoint_coe
rag.content:
@[simp, norm_cast]
theorem disjoint_coe : Disjoint (a : α) b ↔ Disjoint a b := by
  rw [disjoint_iff, disjoint_iff, ← coe_inf, ← coe_bot, coe_inj]

informal_statement: Given two disjoint sets $X$ and $Y$, converting an element of $X \oplus Y$ to an element of $(X \cup Y)$ and back to $X \oplus Y$ yields the original element.
informal_proof: Let $X$ and $Y$ be disjoint sets, meaning they share no common elements. Consider an element $i$ that belongs to either $X$ or $Y$ but not both, due to the disjointness of $X$ and $Y$. When we convert $i$ into $(X \cup Y).Elem$ format, we retain its origin in either $X$ or $Y$. When converting back to $X \oplus Y$, we reconstruct $i$ precisely as it was, whether from $X$ or $Y$, because the disjointness ensures no ambiguity arises during this process. Thus, the conversions preserve the original element.

id.name: toUnion_toSum
id.content:
/-- Converting `X.Elem ⊕ Y.Elem` to `(X ∪ Y).Elem` and back to `X.Elem ⊕ Y.Elem` gives the original element, assuming that
`X` and `Y` are disjoint. -/
lemma toUnion_toSum {X Y : Set α} [∀ a, Decidable (a ∈ X)] [∀ a, Decidable (a ∈ Y)] (hXY : X ⫗ Y) (i : X.Elem ⊕ Y.Elem) :
    i.toUnion.toSum = i := by
  rw [Set.disjoint_right] at hXY
  cases i <;> simp [Subtype.toSum, Sum.toUnion, HasSubset.Subset.elem, hXY]

C1_dependencies.name: Set
C1_dependencies.content:
/-- A set is a collection of elements of some type `α`.

Although `Set` is defined as `α → Prop`, this is an implementation detail which should not be
relied on. Instead, `setOf` and membership of a set (`∈`) should be used to convert between sets
and predicates.
-/
def Set (α : Type u) := α → Prop
